the reason that .save() in .post() was wrapped inside a transaction was so it would automatically retry on retriable errors. Does this code do that?
No, the original code does not automatically retry on transient errors. Wrapping .save() inside User.db.transaction() will actually throw a runtime error rather than enable retries.
Here is why it fails and how Mongoose transactions actually work:
Mongoose's db property (the native MongoDB Db instance) does not expose a .transaction() helper method. Calling User.db.transaction(...) results in a TypeError: User.db.transaction is not a function.

The MongoDB native Node.js driver has a helper method called withTransaction() attached to Client Sessions (not the Db or Model object). withTransaction() is what automatically handles transient transaction errors and commit retries.
Single .save() operations do not require transactions:
In MongoDB, any single-document operation (like save() or insertOne()) is already atomic. Wrapping a single .save() in a transaction adds multi-document overhead without providing additional safety.
How to Implement Automatic Retries Correctly

can gets, puts, or deletes have similar transient transaction problems?

No, GET operations do not have transient transaction/write conflict problems. However, PUT and DELETE operations can encounter transient errors when written to execute inside transactions or under high-concurrency conditions.
Here is how transient errors affect each HTTP verb in MongoDB and Mongoose:
Transient Transaction Problems: No. Read operations do not modify state or acquire write locks, so they do not suffer from Write Conflicts or TransientTransactionError failures.

Network Blips: Like any database operation, a GET query can occasionally fail due to brief network disruptions. However, because reads are idempotent (they don't change state), you can safely re-run a GET query without side effects.
2. PUT and DELETE Requests (Write & Delete Operations)
Transient Transaction Problems: Yes. Both PUT and DELETE perform writes on MongoDB documents, meaning they can encounter transient failure scenarios:

Write Conflicts: If two concurrent requests try to update or delete the exact same document at the same time inside a transaction, MongoDB aborted one transaction with a TransientTransactionError to prevent dirty writes.
Document Versioning Failures: If you use optimistic concurrency control (e.g., Mongoose's { __v } version key), concurrent updates will fail with a VersionError, which requires a retry.

Handling Retries for PUT and DELETE
Because PUT and DELETE are idempotent (performing the exact same update or deletion twice yields the same end state), they are safer candidates for automatic retry logic than POST.

I can't find the tasks collection in MongoDB Atlas dashboard. What are some specific instuctions to get there? Especially if I didn't manually define the clusters
Finding collections in MongoDB Atlas when you didn't manually set up the cluster layout can be tricky because the UI layout has changed over time.
Here are step-by-step instructions to locate your database, collection, and the Indexes tab:
On the left-hand sidebar or the main Database overview page, look for your active cluster (usually named something like Cluster0 by default).
Right on the cluster card, click the Browse Collections button (or click Collections in the top cluster navigation bar).
Once inside the Collections tab, you will see a tree view on the left listing your databases (e.g., test or whatever database name your Mongoose connection string uses).
Click on your database name to expand it.

You should see your collections listed underneath: users and tasks. (Note: If you haven't successfully created a task yet, the tasks collection might not appear until Mongoose creates it on the first write. If you don't see it, try running a task creation request once, then refresh the Atlas page).
Once you have clicked on the tasks collection, look at the sub-tabs near the top of the main panel. You will see tabs like Documents, Indexes, Aggregation, etc.
You will see a list of indexes (by default, there's always _id_). Look for any other index that was previously created on name or deadline.
Click the Drop (or trash/delete) button next to those old indexes to remove them.
Alternative / Easiest Shortcut: Drop the Database

If you are having trouble navigating the Atlas UI to find specific indexes, it is often much faster to drop the entire database so MongoDB completely wipes and recreates it with clean defaults the next time your app runs:
In the Collections view where your databases are listed on the left, hover over your database name.
Click the three dots or the trash can icon next to the database name.
Type in the name of the database to confirm deletion and click Drop Database.
Restart your Node server and re-run your test suite. Your app will automatically recreate the users and tasks collections using your updated, index-free Mongoose schemas!
